data: Soviet Moon rocket; four launches all failed
Skeleton entry for /fleet (PRD-012 v0.2 / Phase A scaffold). Builder + agency + first-flight per public sources. Specs and gallery TBD in later phases.

The N1 was the Soviet Union's Saturn V — and the reason it never reached the Moon. Standing 105 metres tall, its first stage clustered thirty engines around its base, not by choice but by necessity: no single Soviet engine came close to the power of the American F-1, so Korolev's team ganged thirty smaller ones together and hoped they would fire in concert. They never did. With no test stand large enough to fire the assembled stage on the ground, every launch was the first full test of the propulsion system — and all four, between 1969 and 1972, failed. The second launch (N1-5L, 3 July 1969) fell back onto its pad in one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded. Its NK-33 engines, hidden away after the programme was cancelled, proved among the finest ever built and flew on American rockets a quarter-century later — a brilliant machine beaten by the one thing it was never allowed to do: be tested before it flew.

The Soviet Union’s answer to Saturn V — a 105 m super-heavy rocket with thirty NK-15 engines on the first stage. All four launches between 1969 and 1972 failed; the program was cancelled when Apollo 17 ended any chance of a Soviet crewed lunar landing.
